newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Jobs, GDP and the elections.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD/Jobs, GDP and the elections.

text.p: Wall Street faces an exceptionally heavy slate of economic data but with national elections little more than a week away, only the rudest of surprises is apt to stir the market to decisive action.

Even a short list of the headline figures due is a weighty one. Monthly figures include the October wages and payrolls report and the National Association of Purchasing Management (NAPM) index as well as September leading economic indicators.
Markets will also get their first look at the third quarter's Gross Domestic Product and Employment Cost Index.

Ultimately, the market will be seeking the answer to the same question that has dogged it all year: Will the Fed see in the numbers the inflation signal it has been watching for? "The importance of all these numbers is conditioned on what they mean to the Fed," said Larry Wachtel, market analyst at Prudential Securities. "So far what's happening looks like what Greenspan warned us about in July, that the economy would decelerate later in the year."

During another month, in another year, the prospect of a looming NAPM index or payrolls report would dominate the psyche of the market, unleasing a torrent of buying or selling on occasions when the data surprise.
But this week analysts expect otherwise, anticipating that the tone of the market -- which crept steadily lower last week -- will likely remain cautious until clear of the elections.
"The election will keep people sidelined to some degree," said Wachtel. "We love the split-screen and the gridlock, so a Democratic sweep (of the Presidency and Congress) could really hurt badly."
The Dow industrials slid 87 points last week, closing lower on each day except Friday.
While Wall Street is keeping a cautious demeanor, analysts have noted several differences between this race for the White House and the one that took place four years ago.

"This election is certainly different from the last one because, number one, I don't think anyone thinks Dole has a chance," said Amas Securities Chief Executive Peggy Farley. "That means we're pretty confident we'll have four more years of the same thing."

While market watchers have individual preferences for one piece of information or another, analysts consistently name monthly payrolls, wages and unemployment figures as being most apt to move the market if they vary from forecasts because wage costs are viewed as a key leading inflation indicator.

Economists expect the nation's unemployment rate to hold steady at 5.2 percent for October and average hourly earnings are seen rising by 0.4 percent, a trace lower than their 0.5 percent rise a month earlier.

Non-farm payrolls are another story, however, with economists forecasting payrolls to grow by 220,000 after falling by 40,000 in September. The prospect is not shaking Wall Street because September's dip is considered an anomaly.

The NAPM index is expected to edge lower to 51.0 from 51.7 in September, indicating modest expansion in the manufacturing sector and the third quarter Employment Cost Index is seen posting a 0.8 percent rise, matching a quarter ago.
Other reports due for release this week include September personal income and consumption, new home sales and factory orders and the October consumer confidence index.

While many of the largest companies have now weighed in with quarterly corporate earnings reports, many still remain. Some scheduled to report this week, with estimates and comparable results, include:
